policy_title: Boost Cancer Survival Rates and 62-Day Treatment Guarantee
stated: Boost cancer survival rates by: Introducing a guarantee that 100% of patients will be able to start treatment within 62 days from urgent referral, replacing ageing radiotherapy machines and increasing their number, recruiting more cancer nurses, passing a Cancer Survival Research Act, and halving the time for new treatments to reach patients by expanding the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency’s capacity. Also launching a new prostate cancer screening programme for those at higher risk.

source.quote: Boost cancer survival rates and introduce a guarantee for 100% of patients to start treatment for cancer within 62 days from urgent referral. Boost cancer survival rates by: Introducing a guarantee that 100% of patients will be able to start treatment within 62 days from urgent referral. Replacing ageing radiotherapy machines and increasing their number, so no one has to travel too far for treatment. Recruiting more cancer nurses so that every patient has a dedicated specialist supporting them throughout their treatment. Passing a Cancer Survival Research Act requiring the Government to coordinate and ensure funding for research into the cancers with the lowest survival rates. Halving the time for new treatments to reach patients by expanding the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency’s capacity. Launching a new prostate cancer screening programme for those at higher risk.

bearing_set.reason: Directly targets NHS cancer treatment access, waiting times, radiotherapy capacity, nurse recruitment, and screening — core healthcare access and capacity indicators.

membership_note: This is a genuinely single-target policy: all five sub-measures are designed to improve cancer diagnosis, treatment access, and survival, which lands squarely on O3 (Healthcare). Potential fiscal costs exist (machines, nurses, screening) but the policy gives no funding mechanism, so a public-finances bearing (O12) cannot be grounded beyond speculation. A secondary prosperity effect (improved workforce participation from better survival rates) is real but too diffuse and marginal relative to the baseline to clear the non-negligible bar for O13.
